analysis.one_liner: Exempts smaller banks and non-financial companies from the Volcker Rule's ban on banks' speculative trading.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in November 2015 and died there when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Volcker Rule, part of the post-2008 Dodd-Frank law, bans banks from making speculative trades with their own money and from owning or sponsoring hedge funds and private equity funds. This bill would exempt banks with $10 billion or less in assets from the rule entirely, and would also exempt non-financial companies and any company merely because it controls one. It never got a committee hearing or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks with $10 billion or less in assets, which would be freed from the rule's restrictions and compliance costs, and non-financial companies that own or sponsor hedge funds or private equity funds, which would no longer count as regulated 'banking entities'.

how_it_helps.text: Banks with total consolidated assets of $10 billion or less would be entirely exempt from the Volcker Rule's trading and fund-ownership restrictions.

Companies not predominantly engaged in financial activities — and any entity that counts as a 'banking entity' only because it controls such a company — would be carved out of the rule, along with their subsidiaries.

analysis.who_pays: If banks insured and backed by the federal safety net resume speculative trading, losses and instability fall partly on depositors, taxpayers who stand behind deposit insurance, and the wider financial system. Customers see little direct gain.

drawbacks.text: The bill's own good-faith case is real: the Volcker Rule's compliance costs fall hardest on community and regional banks that do little proprietary trading, and supporters argued a blanket exemption for smaller banks would relieve that burden.

Exempting banks with up to $10 billion in assets from a rule meant to keep government-backstopped banks out of speculative trading removes one guardrail, shifting risk toward the deposit insurance fund and taxpayers if losses occur.
The carve-out for non-financial companies and their subsidiaries would let some firms escape the rule's restrictions on owning or sponsoring hedge funds and private equity funds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for relief from compliance costs on small banks is genuine, but the bill was a broad carve-out rather than a calibrated fix, and it went well beyond community banks by rewriting who counts as a 'banking entity'. Given how the rule actually burdens trading-heavy big banks most, the costs of losing the guardrail outweighed the modest benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never came up again before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mia Love introduced the bill on November 17, 2015, joined by Reps. Neugebauer and Huizenga of Michigan.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
That was the last action on the bill; it received no committee vote, no floor vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, both Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one is better off because it died — it simply never moved. Had it passed, small banks and companies sponsoring private funds would have gained a deregulation whose risks fell on the broader public.

for.name: Rep. Mia Love
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt smaller banks and non-financial companies from the Volcker Rule.

for.name: Reps. Neugebauer and Huizenga
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only cosponsors.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters — the sponsor and both cosponsors — were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill and no vote was ever taken.

industries.industry: Banks with $10 billion or less in assets
industries.note: The bill would free these banks entirely from the Volcker Rule, cutting their compliance costs but letting government-backstopped banks return to speculative trading whose downside falls on depositors and taxpayers.

industries.industry: Non-financial companies that own or sponsor hedge funds and private equity funds
industries.note: The bill rewrites who counts as a 'banking entity' so these firms and their subsidiaries escape the rule's ban on fund ownership and sponsorship, reopening a Dodd-Frank loophole.

The bill does nothing for big banks — the main targets of the Volcker Rule — which would remain subject to it; large banks that had pushed for Volcker relief generally preferred broader repeal than this bill offered.
